Q: EF Core migration fails with SqlException: there is already an object named 'Courses' in the database after resetting migrations A:

This error occurs because Entity Framework (EF) Core is attempting to create a table named Courses, but a table or object with that exact name already exists in your SQL Server database.

This most commonly happens when the database schema has desynchronised from your Entity Framework migrations history.

What is the recommended/best practice approach to resolve this issue?

The recommended best practice to resolve this issue depends on whether you are using Entity Framework (EF) Core Migrations or executing a raw SQL script.

If I don't care about preserving the data during local development, what is the cleanest way to sync EF Core with the database?

If you do not care about keeping the data currently in your local or test database, wiping it is the cleanest solution. Run Drop-Database in the Package Manager Console (or dotnet ef database drop in the CLI). Run Update-Database (or dotnet ef database update) to recreate everything smoothly from scratch.

How can I baseline the existing database state with the new Fresh Start migration without dropping the existing tables/data?

If you cannot delete the database, you need to tell Entity Framework that the Courses table is already there, so it skips the creation step:

  1. Generate an Empty Migration (The "Ignore" Method). Temporarily comment out the DbSet<Course> property in your DbContext class. Add a new migration: Add-Migration IgnoreCoursesTable. This creates an empty migration file. Uncomment the DbSet<Course> property in your DbContext. Run Add-Migration Initial (or a new name). The upcoming changes will now ignore the creation of Courses. Run Update-Database to apply any remaining changes.

  2. Manually Fake the Migration in the Database. If this is your very first migration (Initial), but the database tables were already created manually: Comment out the code inside the Up() method of your migration file (specifically the migrationBuilder.CreateTable(name: "Courses", ...) block). Run Update-Database. This will successfully create the __EFMigrationsHistory table and insert a row stating this migration has been applied, without executing the failing SQL commands. Revert the comments in your migration file, so it remains an accurate reference of your schema.

Double-check your application's appsettings.json file. Make sure your Connection String is pointing to your intended target database and not a production or shared database by mistake.

For further reading and detailed explanation of the EF Core Migration see the linked resource.

Q: How should a table reference two columns that have a many-to-many relationship? A:

Presuming your Brands and Suppliers tables are defined as such:

CREATE TABLE Brands (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE Suppliers (
    ID   INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name CHAR(80) NOT NULL
);

Your bridge table BrandsSuppliers should be constructed this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    PRIMARY KEY (BrandID, SupplierID),

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID)
);

We use composite primary key (BrandID, SupplierID) with each component referencing to 2 other table's PKs, that is the simplest way to ensure itself's uniqueness, and it also ensure as long as a row (or pair) in this table exists, the relative brand and supplier must exist. We can of course create its own primary key ID but since this table totally depends on the other two, there's no point to add another new column for such purpose. Also, using a separate stand-alone PK would requires us to add another constraint to ensure the row's uniqueness. (explained below)

And this is how your Products table can directly reference the bridge table (AKA junction table):

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

It's quite straightforward. However, there are times when we need to write queries which need to JOIN between Products and Brands tables, or bwteen Products and Suppliers table. Without direct FK/PK relationship between the two tables, it's still valid to use JOIN clause but it would not leverage the relationship directly. So it would be a better idea to add the FK/PK relationship between Products and Brands, as well as between Products and Suppliers, like so:

CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID         INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name       CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID    INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Product_BrandSupplier
        FOREIGN KEY (BrandID, SupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(BrandID, SupplierID)
);

Adding the 2 FK references also makes relationship clearer for those who read the schema.

What if BrandsSuppliers has its own PK column

It can have its own primary key, maybe like this way:

CREATE TABLE BrandsSuppliers (
    ID         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BrandID    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)    REFERENCES Brands(ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID) REFERENCES Suppliers(ID),

    CONSTRAINT UQ_BrandSupplier UNIQUE (BrandID, SupplierID)  -- needed by many-to-many relationship
);

We need to add that UNIQUE constraint to ensure the row (relationship) is unqiue because many-to-many relationship demands that.

And now we might be tempted to change the design of Products table like so:

-- NOTE: this is a bad idea
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandID         INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    SupplierID      INTEGER  NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandID)         REFERENCES Brands(ID), -- Same as before
    FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID)      REFERENCES Suppliers(ID), -- Same as before
    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID) -- Changed
);

However, this would bring a new problem. It is highly possible that the certain product could reference to a book not in the brand-supplier relationship, or the supplier is missing in the relationship. This is problematic. We are thus forced to remove those 2 FK/PK relationship and consequently the 2 columns as well, like so:

-- Better, but not good enough.
CREATE TABLE Products (
    ID              INTEGER  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name            CHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    BrandSupplierID INTEGER  NOT NULL,

    FOREIGN KEY (BrandSupplierID) REFERENCES BrandsSuppliers(ID)
);

That means if we need to look up a product's brand info or the supplier info, we must route through the BrandsSuppliers table first. It would be 2 JOIN clauses instead of just 1. So, using composite primary key in BrandsSuppliers table is a better solution.

Q: VSCode Spring Initializr Error: Can running but package and import still red A:

VS Studio doesn't recognize your .java files as a sources and treated them as text. Either you incorrectly configured and imported your project from Maven to VS Studio, or didn't specify the source path for your .java files.

Here is a tutorial how to import existing Maven pgoject to VS Studio.

Q: how to add header to fetch GET method A:

Headers are attached the same way for GET and POST. Your code is structurally correct.

Two errors you can fix

Typo X-Aequseted-With → X-Requested-With

If you're testing against api.github.com specifically, its CORS preflight only allows a specific set of headers, and X-CSRF-TOKEN isn't one of them, so the browser blocks the request before it's sent. Against your own backend, you control this via Access-Control-Allow-Headers on the server.

For bearer-token auth, use the Authorization header instead of X-CSRF-TOKEN

headers: {
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
  "Accept": "application/json",
  "Authorization": `Bearer ${token}`
}

Q: Spring boot does not show custom error when exception is thrown A:

You missed

@ResponseBody on method

or return

ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse>

Q: JMeter Basic Authentication with HTTP Authorization Manager A:

If you use httpclient.parameters - make sure that you have HTTPClient3 implementation of the HTTP Request Sampler(s).

Double check that HTTP Authorization Manager really adds "Authorization" header and credentials are correct.

See How to use HTTP Basic Authentication in JMeter for example of bypassing basic HTTP authentication in phpmyadmin.

Q: .Getting a java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: org.objectweb.asm.ClassWriter.<init>(Z)V in my spring hibernate application A:

NoSuchMethodError is thrown mainly because you have incompatible version and version mismatches in dependecies specified in gradle or other dependency managent tool's script.

So take your time re-evaluate your dependencies, compatiblities and versions. Im sure this will fix it up.

A more detailed description can be found in here. Docker Image of Jersey Web Application

Q: How to use TLS with non RTOS A:

Mongoose https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose is a TCP/IP stack capable of running on both RTOS and non-RTOS environments. Here is a working baremetal example on STM32F4 :

https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/tree/master/tutorials/stm32/nucleo-f429zi/minimal

Make sure you have GNU make and ARM GCC installed, then simply type "make build flash" in that directory. Attach serial console to see the board's IP address (it should take it from DHCP).

Once done, you can easily add TLS. Add keys, like here https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/blob/53d2356472e4a475ef92425d6372c2c0e36b0e61/tutorials/http/http-restful-server/main.c#L34-L50
Then, add a TLS handshake: https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/blob/53d2356472e4a475ef92425d6372c2c0e36b0e61/tutorials/http/http-restful-server/main.c#L55-L64
Then, add HTTPS listener: https://github.com/cesanta/mongoose/blob/53d2356472e4a475ef92425d6372c2c0e36b0e61/tutorials/http/http-restful-server/main.c#L98

And that's the way you should get it.

If you want to do the same under Cube MX, follow the ST KB article to integrate Mongoose into the CubeMX project: https://community.st.com/stm32-mcus-60/stm32h7-ethernet-with-mongoose-getting-started-guide-165096 and repeat the 3 steps above.
